This document forms the core of my forthcoming habilitation thesis, presenting self-contained original results accompanied by rigorous proofs. Driven by the need to analyze data residing on Riemannian manifolds, these works aim to develop general, meaningful, and applicable tools for modeling and learning from "Riemannian data," as well as analyzing associated algorithms for sampling, optimization, and stochastic approximation. Because the Riemannian setting often differs significantly from its Euclidean counterpart, this divergence generates the mathematical challenges addressed in this thesis. The initial chapter offers custom geometric constructions for use throughout the work, while the four subsequent chapters tackle unresolved issues identified in recent literature. Additionally, a one-page guide outlining how to read the thesis is located immediately after the table of contents.

The spectral slope of Magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) turbulence varies depending on the adopted spectral theory: the Kraichnan-Iroshnikov-Dobrowolny (KID) theory yields a slope of $-3/2$, while Marsch-Matthaeus-Zhou's and Goldreich-Sridhar frameworks—often referred to as Kolmogorov-like (K-41 like) MHD theory—result in a $-5/3$ slope. Other approaches, such as Biskamp's, consider combinations of these $-5/3$ and $-3/2$ scales. Establishing rigorous mathematical proofs for any of these theories holds significant scientific value. Building upon the 2012 study by A. Biryuk and W. Craig (*Physica D* 241, 426–438), this work rigorously derives inertial range bounds for K-41 like behavior in MHD turbulence, explicitly formulating the upper and lower limits within which the spectral slope scales as $-5/3$. Furthermore, we demonstrate that Leray weak solutions of the standard MHD model are bounded in Fourier space, that the system's spectral energy is bounded, and that its time average diminishes over time.

Operators characterized by zero-dimensional spectral measures arise intrinsically within the framework of ergodic Schrödinger operators. We introduce the notion of a complete family of Hausdorff measure functions to examine and differentiate these measures with arbitrary precision. We demonstrate that for half-line operators possessing a positive upper Lyapunov exponent, the dimension of their spectral measures is logarithmic at most, regardless of the specific boundary phase. We establish the optimality of this bound by providing a concrete example of an operator whose spectral measure achieves this dimension. Furthermore, we generalize and refine foundational results from rank one perturbation theory and quantum dynamics to accommodate generalized Hausdorff dimensions.

This study examines the fluctuations and dissipation characteristics of a string situated in a finite-temperature, finite-density, deformed anti-de Sitter (AdS) space, realized as a charged black hole within the Einstein-Maxwell-Dilaton framework. We explicitly account for the backreaction on the horizon function resulting from the exponential deformation of the AdS geometry. Within this model, we determine the admittance and analyze how chemical potential and temperature affect it. Furthermore, we compute the two-point correlation functions and mean square displacements for both bosonic and fermionic systems to derive short- and long-time approximations. In the long-time limit, the system exhibits a sub-diffusive behavior scaling as $\sim \log t$. Finally, by integrating the admittance results with those from the correlation functions, we verify the fluctuation-dissipation theorem for bosonic and fermionic contexts.

This paper introduces the notion of weak sharp minima (WSM) within the context of convex interval-valued functions (IVFs). To characterize the WSM set of a convex IVF, the authors provide both primal and dual descriptions. The primal characterization utilizes $gH$-directional derivatives, whereas the dual characterizations rely on newly introduced concepts: the support function for subsets of $I(\mathbb{R})^{n}$ and $gH$-subdifferentiability applied to convex IVFs. Additionally, the study establishes a necessary $gH$-subdifferential calculus for convex IVFs, which is subsequently employed to derive dual characterizations for the WSM set.

Multi-modality datasets offer complementary insights for clinical prediction, yet missing data within clinical cohorts restricts the applicability of multi-modal learning. Existing methods struggle with imputing such gaps, particularly when data is missing across heterogeneous modalities (e.g., image versus non-image) or when a single modality is substantially absent. This study tackles missing data imputation by modeling the joint distribution of multi-modal inputs. Inspired by the partial bidirectional generative adversarial net (PBiGAN), we introduce a Conditional PBiGAN (C-PBiGAN) designed to impute one modality using conditional information from another. Specifically, C-PBiGAN incorporates a conditional latent space within a missing data framework that jointly encodes available multi-modal inputs and applies a class regularization loss to the imputed data to recover discriminative features. To the best of our knowledge, this marks the first generative adversarial approach to address multi-modal missing imputation by explicitly modeling the joint distribution of image and non-image data. Our model's efficacy was validated using both the National Lung Screening Trial (NLST) dataset and an external clinical cohort. Results demonstrate that C-PBiGAN yields significant improvements in lung cancer risk estimation over representative imputation methods; for instance, AUC values rose by 2.9% in the NLST and 4.3% in our internal dataset compared to standard PBiGAN, with a statistical significance of p<0.05.

Spontaneous parametric down-conversion (SPDC) serves as a dependable method for creating entangled states, typically requiring a coherent laser beam to pump a nonlinear crystal. In this study, we overcome this constraint by utilizing a commercial light-emitting diode (LED) as the pump source to produce polarization-entangled photon pairs. This approach defies conventional expectations, given the LED's extremely low spatial coherence; however, this lack of coherence is preserved within the resulting biphoton wavefunction. Nevertheless, type-II phase-matching inherently selects only specific LED frequencies and wavelengths for the down-conversion process, enabling the generation of localized polarization Bell states even amidst global incoherence across the transverse plane. In our experiments, we evaluated the degree of polarization entanglement induced by the LED using the standard framework of Bell inequality violations. We obtained a Bell value of $S=2.33\pm 0.097$, which clearly exceeds the classical limit of $S=2$, thereby confirming the presence of quantum entanglement. This research suggests that other natural light sources, including sunlight and bioluminescence, could also be harnessed to prepare polarization entanglement, potentially paving the way for electricity-free quantum communication in outer space.

This technical report outlines the model submitted by the Chung-Ang University and Korea University (CAU_KU) team for Track 1 (Low-quality fake audio detection) of the Audio Deep Synthesis Detection (ADD) 2022 Challenge. To address the challenges posed by low-quality audio environments, we introduced a frequency feature masking (FFM) augmentation technique designed to facilitate the application of spectrogram-based models. We implemented both FFM and mixup augmentations across five high-performing deep neural network architectures, utilizing mel-spectrogram and constant Q transform (CQT) features for spoofing detection. Our top-ranked submission achieved an Equal Error Rate (EER) of 23.8%, securing 3rd place in Track 1.

Theories regarding the spontaneous collapse of the wavefunction attempt to explain why quantum mechanics might fail at macroscopic scales, yet definitive tests have been blocked by the difficulty of detecting predicted collapse signals above background noise. We propose to address this obstacle by using a superconducting qubit to accurately measure the heat generated in a mechanical resonator due to collapse. We demonstrate that strong coupling between the qubit and resonator allows for both rapid measurements and efficient initialization of the qubit near its ground state; combined, these factors significantly reduce the impact of quasiparticle heating in the qubit, which is the anticipated primary source of noise. Furthermore, we find that bulk acoustic wave resonances can enhance collapse-induced heating through their extremely low dissipation. Collectively, these approaches may make a conclusive verification of collapse models feasible.

This study examines the generalization error of two-layer neural networks applied to determining the ground state of the Schr\"odinger operator within a $d$-dimensional hypercube. We demonstrate that, assuming a priori that the ground state resides in a spectral Barron space, the convergence rate of the generalization error remains independent of the dimension $d$. To substantiate this assumption, we establish a novel regularity estimate for the ground state within the spectral Barron space, a result derived through a fixed-point argument grounded in the Krein-Rutman theorem.

Cyclotron Radiation Emission Spectroscopy (CRES) is a contemporary technique for measuring charged particle energies through precise frequency analysis of emitted cyclotron radiation. For CRES setups involving gas within the fiducial volume, signal and noise behavior can be described using a hidden Markov model. We present a new application of the Viterbi algorithm to establish informational limits on the optimal detection of cyclotron radiation signals in gas-filled CRES experiments. This yields specific constraints that guide the development of future reconstruction algorithms and detector designs. The effectiveness of the resulting decision rules has been validated using both Monte Carlo simulations and Project 8 data.

Utilizing both probabilistic and analytic methods derived from potential theory, this study examines Dirichlet problems linked to the Dunkl Laplacian $\Delta_k$. Under specific constraints on the open domain $D\subset\R^d$, we demonstrate that a unique continuous function $h$ exists; it is continuous on the closure of $D$, twice differentiable within $D$, satisfies $\Delta_kh=0$ in $D$, and matches the continuous boundary function $f$ on $\partial D$. Furthermore, a probabilistic representation is provided for the solution $h$.

We propose exploration potential, a metric that quantifies the extent to which a reinforcement learning agent has explored its environment class. Unlike information gain, this metric incorporates the environment's reward structure, resulting in an exploration criterion that is both necessary and sufficient for achieving asymptotic optimality (acting optimally across the entire environment class). Through experiments with multi-armed bandits, we utilize exploration potential to demonstrate how various algorithms balance the tradeoff between exploration and exploitation.

Advanced battery management systems function like the brain for lithium-ion batteries, relying heavily on battery models that balance speed and accuracy. Currently, mainstream equivalent circuit models and electrochemical models fail to fully meet this requirement, struggling with either computational complexity or predictive precision. This issue has become increasingly critical for emerging applications, such as electric vertical take-off and landing (eVTOL) aircraft, which operate across wide current ranges and lack suitable models in existing literature. To address this gap, this study introduces an innovative model named BattX. BattX is an equivalent circuit model designed to emulate the advantages of single particle models with electrolyte and thermal dynamics, resulting in a system that is both computationally efficient and physically interpretable while maintaining high accuracy. By employing multiple circuits to approximate key electrochemical and physical processes during charge and discharge cycles, the model enables a comprehensive experimental strategy to identify parameters in groups from data. Experimental validation confirms that BattX can accurately predict voltages across a broad spectrum of low to high C-rates.

In High Energy Physics (HEP), jets consist of correlated particle collections generated ubiquitously during particle collisions, such as those at CERN's Large Hadron Collider (LHC). While machine learning (ML) generative models, including generative adversarial networks (GANs), hold the promise of substantially speeding up LHC jet simulations, no such models currently exist that utilize jets' natural representation as a particle cloud (a set of particles in momentum space). This study introduces the JetNet particle cloud dataset and applies established point cloud GANs to it. Evaluation metrics include (1) 1-Wasserstein distances between high- and low-level feature distributions, (2) a newly proposed Fr\'{e}chet ParticleNet Distance, and (3) coverage and (4) minimum matching distance metrics. Our findings indicate that existing GANs are insufficient for physics applications; consequently, we developed a new Message Passing GAN (MPGAN). This MPGAN surpasses existing point cloud GANs on nearly all metrics and demonstrates significant potential for HEP. We present JetNet as an innovative point-cloud dataset for the ML community and establish MPGAN as a benchmark for future improvements. Furthermore, to enhance accessibility and reproducibility, we have released an open-source JetNet Python package featuring interfaces for particle cloud datasets, evaluation and loss metric implementations, and other utilities to support ML development in HEP.

Resource-constrained networked autonomous systems must balance task effectiveness with efficient resource usage, where conserving resources often degrades performance. This work focuses on developing strategies to manage communication costs related to measurements between agents. A standard method for balancing communication overhead with estimation accuracy is event triggering (ET), which transmits data only when necessary, such as when Kalman filter innovations surpass a defined threshold. When direct measurements are unavailable, agents can leverage implicit information to achieve performance nearly equivalent to that obtained through continuous explicit data sharing. However, currently, there are no methods for establishing such thresholds with formal guarantees regarding task performance. To address this, we propose a new belief space discretization technique that abstracts continuous dynamics into a discrete Markov decision process, scalable for handling threshold-dependent ET estimator error covariances. By applying an existing probabilistic trade-off analysis tool, we determine the full set of optimal balances between resource consumption and task success. From these results, a specific ET threshold selection strategy is derived. Simulations demonstrate that this approach effectively identifies meaningful trade-offs between performance and energy savings with minimal computational cost.

Inferring galaxy attenuation curves frequently relies on spectral energy distribution (SED) modeling, in which dust attenuation is estimated concurrently with other physical properties. This study evaluates how effectively SED modeling can derive these curves from broadband photometry and proposes a novel, flexible model that significantly enhances the accuracy of attenuation curve determination. By fitting mock SEDs produced by the Simba cosmological simulation using the Prospector code, we assess this approach. While examining the widely used uniform screen assumption, we introduce a new non-uniform screen model defined by the proportion of unobscured stellar light. This approach permits a fraction of starlight to pass through unattenuated, yielding a more adaptable attenuation curve by separating UV and optical curve shapes. Employing the non-uniform screen model substantially improves the constraints on the dust attenuation curve, reducing the median offset in UV attenuation from -0.30 dex under the uniform screen assumption to -0.17 dex with the new model. This increased accuracy in modeling dust attenuation also refines inferred star formation rates (SFRs), lowering the average SFR offset by 0.12 dex. Finally, we discuss the effectiveness of this improved model, addressing limitations related to star-dust geometries and the constraints imposed by available SED observations.

Electron beam ion sources (EBISs) function on the principle of electron impact ionization, making them ideal for generating ions with very high charges. These sources can produce DC ion beams as well as ion pulses with varying temporal structures. Compared to many other ion sources, EBISs provide ion beams characterized by low energy spread and superior beam emittances. Additionally, highly charged ions generated within these systems serve as excellent sources of photons across the spectrum, including X-rays, ultraviolet, extreme ultraviolet, and visible light. This chapter reviews the physics and operating principles of EBISs along with established technical implementations. Through specific examples, it examines their performance and highlights their diverse applications in basic research, technology, and medicine.

This paper presents a classical algorithmic method for solving the k-satisfiability (k-SAT) problem, drawn from the principles of quantum amplitude amplification within the growing domain of quantum-inspired classical algorithms. To formulate our approach, we utilize the Universal SAT (UniSAT) model, which reformulates the Boolean satisfiability issue as a non-convex global optimization task over a continuous, real-valued space. Our key innovation applies a conditioning mechanism to the UniSAT objective function designed to amplify the values at optimal solution points. We detail this method, called AmplifySAT, which mirrors a two-step process involving an oracle-like query followed by a reflection about the mean. Finally, we examine potential implementations in both classical digital and analog computing environments, evaluating AmplifySAT's strengths and constraints relative to established non-convex optimization techniques such as simulated annealing and gradient descent.

The tetrablock, denoted by $\overline{\mathbb{E}}$, is defined as the set $\{ x \in {\mathbb{C}}^3: 1-x_1 z - x_2 w + x_3 zw \neq 0 \text{ whenever } |z| < 1, |w| < 1 \}$, possessing fascinating complex-geometric characteristics. It is distinguished as a starlike, polynomially convex set that is nonetheless nonconvex. Its automorphism group is parameterized by ${\mathrm{Aut}~} {\mathbb{D}} \times {\mathrm{Aut}~} {\mathbb{D}} \times {\mathbb{Z}}_2$, and its distinguished boundary $b\overline{\mathbb{E}}$ is homeomorphic to the solid torus $\overline{\mathbb{D}} \times {\mathbb{T}}$. Within this space lies a special subvariety, $\mathcal{R}_{\mathbb{\overline{E}}} = \big\{ (x_{1}, x_{2}, x_{3}) \in \overline{\mathbb{E}} : x_{1}x_{2}=x_{3} \big\}$, known as the royal variety. This variety acts as a complex geodesic for ${\mathbb{E}}$ and remains invariant under all automorphisms of ${\mathbb{E}}$. Leveraging this geometric structure, we formulate a comprehensive and explicit theory for rational maps from the unit disc ${\mathbb{D}}$ to $\overline{\mathbb{E}}$ that map the unit circle ${\mathbb{T}}$ onto the distinguished boundary $b\overline{\mathbb{E}}$, which are termed rational $\mathbb{ \overline{ E}}$-inner functions. We establish that for any nonconstant rational $\mathbb{ \overline{ E}}$-inner function $x$, either its image on the closed disc is contained within $\mathcal{R}_{\mathbb{\overline{E}}} \cap \overline{\mathbb{E}}$, or it intersects the royal variety $\mathcal{R}_{\mathbb{\overline{E}}}$ precisely $deg(x)$ times. Furthermore, we examine the convex subsets of $\mathcal{J}$, the collection of all such rational $\mathbb{ \overline{ E}}$-inner functions, as well as their extreme points.

Research area ontologies have demonstrated significant utility in interpreting and analyzing scholarly datasets. This chapter introduces the Computer Science Ontology (CSO), which stands as the most extensive ontology dedicated to research domains within Computer Science. We examine various applications that leverage CSO to facilitate high-level functions, including topic classification, metadata extraction, and book recommendation.

Conducting differential conductance spectroscopy at high biases, where the applied voltage surpasses the sample's work function, yields an inaccurate representation of the local density of states (LDOS) because the tunneling barrier changes dynamically. While the significant voltage often renders constant-height measurements experimentally unfeasible, making constant-current spectroscopy more practical, the resulting differential conductance in this mode remains an even less reliable indicator of the LDOS due to fluctuations in tip height. This study introduces a normalization protocol designed to extract the true LDOS from high-bias scanning tunneling spectroscopy conducted in either constant-current or constant-height configurations. We further generalize this approach to incorporate the influence of in-plane momentum of the probed states on the total current. The effectiveness of this proposed method is validated through its application to laterally confined field-emission resonances, which manifest as distinct, peak-shaped features with a well-defined in-plane momentum in the spectra.

Recent years have seen numerous successful neural style transfer applications, most of which operate solely within the pixel domain. We contend that this pixel-based representation is unnatural given that paintings are fundamentally composed of brushstrokes. Instead, we propose a method that optimizes parameterized brushstrokes rather than pixels, coupled with a simple differentiable rendering mechanism. This approach markedly enhances visual quality and offers greater control over stylization, allowing users to direct the flow of brushstrokes. Qualitative and quantitative evaluations confirm the effectiveness of our parameterized representation.

Affective polarization—defined as citizens cultivating intense negativity toward out-party policies and members—has grown significantly across numerous democracies. Key drivers include economic distress, social disparity, and conflicts based on group or racial identities, especially when these align with existing party divisions. This study employs a cultural evolution model to explore how these forces interact to produce and sustain such polarization. We demonstrate that economic events can trigger both affective polarization and the sorting of group identities along partisan lines, thereby amplifying pre-existing inequalities between groups. However, we also present a more optimistic finding: adequate redistribution of wealth via public goods can disrupt this feedback loop and curb the escalation of polarization. Finally, we validate key theoretical predictions using survey data examining inter-group polarization, racial sorting, and affective polarization in the United States over the last half-century.

We present the Oracle-MNIST dataset, a benchmark for pattern classification containing 30,222 ancient character images in 10 categories, each sized 28$\times $28 in grayscale. The dataset focuses on the unique challenges of image noise and distortion inherent to these artifacts. Comprising 27,222 training images and 300 test images per class, Oracle-MNIST utilizes the same format as the original MNIST dataset, ensuring seamless compatibility with existing classification systems, while presenting a significantly harder task. The complexity arises from 1) severe and distinct noises accumulated over three millennia of burial and aging, and 2) highly diverse writing styles from ancient China, rendering it an ideal resource for machine learning research. The dataset can be accessed freely at https://github.com/wm-bupt/oracle-mnist.

We introduce Typography-MNIST (TMNIST), a dataset containing 565,292 grayscale images in MNIST format, featuring 1,812 distinct glyphs rendered across 1,355 Google Fonts in various styles. This glyph collection includes common characters from over 150 modern and historical language scripts and symbols, where each font style presents unique subsets of the total 1,812 glyphs. Created within the CognitiveType project, this dataset supports the development of eye-tracking tools for mapping type to cognition in real-time and computational tools for designing typefaces with specific cognitive attributes like readability. Both the dataset and the scripts for generating MNIST-style images of glyphs in different fonts are publicly accessible at https://github.com/aiskunks/CognitiveType.

Addressing 3D molecular structures of varying dimensions represents a growing and vital challenge in machine learning, particularly within drug discovery. Equivariant Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) excel in this domain by simultaneously exploiting both geometric and relational details; they generate expressive representations by propagating information between nodes, utilizing higher-order constructs to accurately capture data geometry, such as directionality in intermediate layers. This study introduces an equivariant GNN that utilizes Cartesian coordinates to explicitly model directionality and employs a novel attention mechanism serving as a content and spatial-dependent filter during inter-node information propagation. We validate the architecture's effectiveness on predicting quantum mechanical properties of small molecules and demonstrate its advantages for macromolecular challenges, such as protein complexes.

Given that early detection and treatment are the most critical aspects of managing cerebral palsy (CP), developing a predictive system that is both efficient and interpretable is vital. This study identifies a notable disparity in movement frequencies between CP-infants and healthy children, a feature that significantly boosts prediction accuracy. Unlike existing deep learning approaches that neglect infant movement frequencies, we introduce a Frequency Attention-Informed Graph Convolutional Network. Validated on the MINI-RGBD and RVI-38 consumer-grade RGB video datasets, our proposed frequency attention module enhances both classification performance and interpretability. Additionally, we implemented a frequency-binning technique that preserves essential joint position data frequencies while eliminating noise. The results demonstrate state-of-the-art performance on both datasets. This research confirms the utility of frequency data for non-intrusive CP prediction and offers a practical solution for facilitating early diagnosis in areas with scarce clinical resources.

This study analyzes the characteristics and evolutionary trends of Bright Central Galaxies (BCGs) and the adjacent intracluster light (ICL) within galaxy clusters identified by the overlapping Dark Energy Survey and Atacama Cosmology Telescope (DES-ACT) surveys, spanning a redshift interval of $0.20 < z < 0.80$. Within clusters having a halo mass log$_{10}(M_{\rm 200m,SZ}$/M$_{\odot}) > 14.4$, our sample reveals no evolution in the ICL's stellar content between 50 and 300 kpc across the observed redshift range. Furthermore, we determined the stellar mass–halo mass (SMHM) relation for the combined BCG+ICL system, discovering that the slope ($\beta$) of the dependency of $M_{\rm 200m,SZ}$ on BCG+ICL stellar mass increases with radius. This radial trend, where outer regions correlate more strongly with the halo than the core, indicates a two-phase growth mechanism: recent growth ($z<2$) takes place primarily outside the BCG's core. Our SMHM relation results show moderate qualitative consistency with the diffuse light levels predicted by the IllustrisTNG 300-1 hydrodynamic simulations; however, the simulated slope is steeper and the intrinsic scatter is reduced, likely due to the lack of projection effects in the simulations. Additionally, the ICL displays a color gradient where the outskirts are bluer than the core. For clusters with lower halo masses (log$_{10}(M_{\rm 200m,SZ}$/M$_{\odot}) < 14.59$), we observe a modest shift in the color gradient's slope over time. Coupled with the lack of stellar mass growth in these systems, this suggests that lower-mass clusters may have experienced more recent growth via tidal stripping compared to their higher-mass counterparts.

This paper establishes completeness results for Bayesian network inference regarding two parameterizations: the count of variables and the topological vertex separation number. To achieve this, we define the parameterized complexity classes $\mathsf{W[1]PP}$ and $\mathsf{XLPP}$, which correspond to $\mathsf{W[1]}$ and $\mathsf{XNLP}$ in the same way that $\mathsf{PP}$ relates to $\mathsf{NP}$. The topological vertex separation number serves as a directed acyclic graph analogue to pathwidth, acting as a more restrictive metric than the frequently cited treewidth. Grounded in a recent conjecture, our completeness findings for this parameter indicate that deterministic inference algorithms likely demand exponential space relative to both pathwidth and, consequently, treewidth. Ultimately, these insights aim to refine our comprehension of the parameterized complexity of Bayesian inference and its associated time and space requirements.

With the global economy moving toward data-centric industries, there is an accelerating need for automated algorithms capable of transforming scanned document images into machine-readable text. While this shift enables data digitization for advanced analytics and significantly reduces the reliance on manual document inspection, optical character recognition (OCR) has historically prioritized character conversion over the semantic extraction of tables. Recognizing tables involves two primary challenges: table detection and structure analysis. Most previous research has addressed only one of these tasks individually, often neglecting real-world conditions such as rotated images or noise artifacts, rather than providing a comprehensive end-to-end solution. Consequently, recent advancements have leaned heavily on deep learning combined with transfer learning for structure recognition to compensate for limited datasets. This paper introduces "Multi-Type-TD-TSR," a multistage pipeline offering a complete end-to-end approach to table recognition. Leveraging state-of-the-art deep learning models for detection, the system distinguishes among three table categories based on border presence. For structure recognition, it employs a deterministic, non-data-driven algorithm applicable across all three types, which is itself supported by two foundational algorithms tailored specifically for unbordered and bordered tables. Evaluated on the ICDAR 2019 Table Structure Recognition dataset, Multi-Type-TD-TSR establishes a new state-of-the-art performance.

Knowledge Graphs like DBpedia and Freebase often suffer from incomplete entity type information, stemming from both automated processes and manual curation. Entity typing addresses this by determining or predicting an entity's semantic class within a KG. This paper introduces *GRAND*, a new method for entity typing that combines various RDF2vec graph walk strategies with textual descriptions of entities. RDF2vec functions by creating graph walks followed by using a language model to derive embeddings for graph nodes. This research highlights that both the specific graph walk generation technique and the choice of embedding model significantly influence performance on entity typing tasks. Consequently, *GRAND* surpasses baseline methods on the DBpedia and FIGER benchmark datasets for both fine-grained and coarse-grained classification. Furthermore, findings indicate that pairing order-aware RDF2vec variants with contextual embeddings from textual descriptions yields optimal results.

Do-calculus enables the estimation of interventional distributions from observed joint probabilities within a specified causal framework. While these rules allow for the derivation of all identifiable causal effects, they do not inherently indicate whether a specific effect is identifiable. Shpitser and Pearl developed an algorithm for identifying joint interventional distributions in causal models with unobserved variables, represented as directed acyclic graphs. This algorithm applies the rules of do-calculus and probability properties iteratively; it either produces an expression for the causal distribution or concludes the effect is non-identifiable if identification fails. This paper introduces the R package *causaleffect*, which implements this algorithm and demonstrates its capabilities through illustrative examples.
For $0 \leq k \leq 2$, we prove unconditional sharp upper bounds on the $k$-th moments of the family of quadratic Dirichlet $L$-functions at the central point.

This paper presents a framework utilizing differential dynamic programming (DDP) to generate polynomial trajectories for differentially flat systems. Departing from conventional approaches that rely on linear equations of increasing size for multiple polynomial segments, this method adopts a state-space perspective. This shifts the problem to a finite horizon control system with a fixed state dimension, automatically satisfying continuity requirements between consecutive polynomials. As a result, constrained trajectory generation—with or without time optimization—can be reformulated as a discrete-time finite-horizon optimal control problem subject to inequality constraints, solvable via the recently developed interior-point DDP (IPDDP) algorithm. Additionally, for unconstrained trajectory generation with preallocated time, the problem is identified as a linear-quadratic tracking (LQT) issue, which corresponds to the DDP algorithm performing a single exact iteration. All proposed algorithms demonstrate linear complexity relative to the number of segments. Numerical comparisons against state-of-the-art techniques and physical experiments are provided to confirm and validate these theoretical results. The implementation code will be made available open-source.

Cosmic rays (CRs) are believed to play a significant role as a feedback mechanism within star-forming galaxies, offering essential pressure support and potentially driving galactic outflows. To examine wind initiation from an initially hydrostatic atmosphere powered by CRs, we conducted multidimensional CR-magnetohydrodynamic simulations that account for both streaming and diffusive transport. By comparing our estimated characteristic Eddington limit—where CR force surpasses gravitational pull—with actual simulated systems, we scaled these findings to conditions found in star-forming galaxies. This analysis suggests that CRs are likely to contribute to outflow driving across a wide spectrum of star formation environments. Furthermore, we quantified the energy and momentum exchange between CRs and gas, as well as mass outflow rates under varying assumptions regarding the relative significance of streaming versus diffusion. Simulations incorporating streaming revealed the emergence and saturation of CR acoustic instability; however, the gas and CRs remained tightly coupled, allowing efficient momentum transfer from CRs to the gas despite the instability. Increased CR fluxes resulted in greater energy transfer to the gas, thereby generating more powerful outflows. In the presence of streaming, the majority of transferred energy manifested as Alfvén wave heating, which elevated gas pressure and internal energy, while only a smaller fraction contributed to the outflow's kinetic energy. Additionally, we investigated runs featuring radiative cooling, which altered gas temperature and pressure distributions but appeared to have minimal impact on mass outflow rates when CR fluxes exceeded the Eddington limit.

By integrating the Halperin-Mazenco formalism with Gross-Pitaevskii theory, we analyze the kinematics and nucleation of quantum vortices in a two-dimensional stirred Bose-Einstein condensate. We define a smooth defect density field to quantify superfluid vorticity, which serves as a topologically conserved quantity. Utilizing this field alongside its associated current density, we investigate pre-nucleation pattern formations within the repulsive potential of an obstacle to identify when vortex nucleation and shedding begin. Our results show that while phase slips occur inside hard potentials even without prior nucleation, in soft potentials they arise only after exceeding a critical stirring velocity that triggers nucleation. Furthermore, the Halperin-Mazenco formalism offers a refined and precise approach for deriving point vortex dynamics directly from the Gross-Pitaevskii equation.

This study examines the numerical resolution of inverse eigenvalue problems through a machine learning lens, focusing on two distinct challenges: the inverse Sturm-Liouville eigenvalue problem involving symmetric potentials and the inverse transmission eigenvalue problem concerning spherically symmetric refractive indices. Initially, we address the associated direct problems to generate the necessary eigenvalue datasets for training the machine learning models. Subsequently, we evaluate various inverse problem scenarios by comparing how effectively different models reconstruct unknown potentials and refractive indices from a limited set of the lowest eigenvalues. The supervised regression techniques employed include k-Nearest Neighbours, Random Forests, and Multi-Layer Perceptrons. Experimental results indicate that, provided their parameters are adequately tuned, these machine learning approaches can successfully solve the investigated inverse eigenvalue problems.

Individuals exhibit varying reactions to inspirational inputs during brainstorming sessions. While prior studies on large-scale ideation systems have explored factors like timing, similarity, and integration, they often neglect individual preferences regarding inspiration. To fill this gap, our research first conducted a co-located brainstorming study with 15 participants, revealing two distinct user archetypes: "inspiration seekers" and "inspiration avoiders." Based on these findings, we developed a user model designed to classify individuals according to their ideation styles, implemented via both rule-based and random forest classifiers. We validated this model through an online experiment involving 380 participants. The results affirmed the existence of these ideator types, demonstrating that seekers gain advantages from inspiration availability, whereas avoiders are detrimentally affected. Notably, the random forest classifier achieved 73% accuracy in identifying user types within just three minutes of ideation. These findings establish the proposed typology as a promising user model for scalable ideation systems. Future work could leverage this distinction to create large-scale platforms that offer more adaptive and personalized inspiration recommendations.

This paper investigates the holographic dual of an asymptotically anti-de Sitter black brane within an Einstein-Yang-Mills framework featuring a non-minimal coupling between Riemann and Yang-Mills fields. We first derive a planar black hole solution for this model up to the first order of $q_2$. Subsequently, we compute the color non-abelian direct current (DC) conductivity and the ratio of shear viscosity to entropy density for this solution. Our findings indicate that the ratio of shear viscosity $\eta$ to entropy density $s$ reaches the Kovtun, Son, and Starinets (KSS) bound, scaling as $\frac{1}{4 \pi}$. However, our calculation for the conductivity provides novel results up to the first order of $q_2$.

Current sign language generation systems often suffer from limited expressivity and unnatural output because they prioritize manual signs while overlooking the grammatical, affective, and semantic roles of facial expressions. This study aims to enhance the semantic representation of sign language by anchoring facial expressions within the generation process. We investigate how modeling the connections among text, glosses, and facial expressions influences sign generation performance. Specifically, we introduce a Dual Encoder Transformer that simultaneously generates manual signs and facial expressions by leveraging similarities and differences identified in text and gloss annotations. Furthermore, this work addresses the role of facial muscle activity in signifying the intensity of manual signs, marking the first application of facial action units in this domain. Experimental results demonstrate that our proposed model significantly improves the quality of automatically generated sign language.

It is widely accepted that a complete theory of quantum gravity must be background independent and possess diffeomorphism invariance. At its broadest scope, diffeomorphism invariance includes field redefinitions, which manifest as diffeomorphisms within the configuration space. We demonstrate that any path-integral formulation of quantum gravity creates a conflict between these two attributes, preventing them from being satisfied at the same time.

The BESIII collaboration leverages $e^+e^-$ collisions within the tau-charm energy range to investigate a diverse array of subjects. These inquiries encompass light mesons and baryons, charmonium (including exotic variants containing charmonium), charmed hadrons, Quantum Chromodynamics, tau physics, and potential new physics discoveries. A corresponding Snowmass white paper details BESIII's achievements and future prospects across these specific domains.

For any two knots, $K$ and $J$, embedded in the three-sphere, we examine the collection of integer quadruples $(g, x, y, z)$ representing a cobordism from $K$ to $J$ with genus $g$ and $x$, $y$, and $z$ critical points of index 0, 1, and 2, respectively. We outline fundamental constraints these sets must adhere to and construct obstructions against their membership, relying on homological invariants derived from cyclic and metacyclic branched coverings. Various examples are provided, culminating in a final case proving that for every pair of integers $g$ and $n$, one can find a ribbon knot $K$ such that any genus $g$ cobordism from $K$ to its mirror image $K^r$ necessitates at least $n$ critical points at each index level.

The heat pulse technique is a standard approach for measuring thermal diffusivity, yet its measurement and analysis become complex when applied to highly porous, heterogeneous materials. This study investigates two open-cell carbon foams that share the same dimensions but differ in porosity. Previous investigations suggested that such complex structures likely exhibit non-Fourier thermal behavior, specifically an 'over-diffusive' propagation mode. The Guyer-Krumhansl continuum equation has emerged as a suitable model for this transient phenomenon. To ensure accurate and reliable thermal parameter extraction, we employed a recently developed, advanced evaluation method based on an analytical solution of the Guyer-Krumhansl equation. Our findings indicate that high porosity alone is a necessary but insufficient condition for observing non-Fourier effects, and that the intensity of these effects depends on porosity levels. Furthermore, some porous samples adhere strictly to the Fourier law. These observations provide a foundation for accurately identifying specific heat transfer mechanisms and their time scales, collectively explaining the observed non-Fourier behavior. Keywords: flash experiments, non-Fourier heat conduction, highly porous carbon foams.

This text presents a comprehensive overview of abelian group theory concepts most pertinent to algebraic topology. It is nearly entirely expository in nature, featuring some unconventional approaches to the discussion of tensor products, torsion products, and $\text{Ext}$ groups.

Accurate and rapid channel estimation is vital for next-generation wireless networks, particularly for supporting diverse vehicular and low-latency applications. Recently, deep learning (DL) techniques have emerged as a promising alternative to traditional least-square (LS) and linear minimum mean square error (LMMSE) methods, with the distinct advantage of not requiring prior knowledge of channel statistics. However, few DL approaches have been successfully implemented on system-on-chip (SoC) hardware, with initial studies indicating that their complexity can surpass that of the entire physical layer, alongside concerns regarding high latency. This paper addresses the design and deployment of an LS-based channel estimation method augmented by deep neural networks (LSDNN) on the Zynq multi-processor SoC (ZMPSoC). Results demonstrate improved performance compared to standard LS and LMMSE schemes. Leveraging software-hardware co-design, word-length optimization, and reconfigurable architectures, we prove that the LSDNN architecture outperforms both LS and LMMSE across various signal-to-noise ratios (SNR), pilot counts, preamble types, and channel conditions. Furthermore, we assess the power, performance, and area (PPA) metrics for both LS and LSDNN applications fabricated as 45 nm ASICs, showing that word-length optimization significantly enhances PPA for the proposed architecture.

Long-lived particles (LLPs) represent a compelling area of research within physics Beyond the Standard Model (BSM), offering significant discovery prospects alongside distinct experimental difficulties. While the Run 2 era of the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) achieved substantial progress in searching for LLPs, numerous key areas of parameter space remain uninvestigated. To fully capitalize on the availability of new data, the advancement and extension of specialized triggers are essential for enhancing LLP detection capabilities. Consequently, the refinement of these triggers has become a central topic in recent literature and during sessions at the LLP@LHC Community workshops and associated experimental groups. This document synthesizes concepts emerging from those workshops and integrates ongoing developments within the trigger communities of experimental collaborations. It outlines the theoretical foundations of various elusive LLP scenarios and evaluates specific trigger strategies that could significantly broaden the reach of LHC investigations. We anticipate that this review will stimulate further innovation among both experimentalists and phenomenologists, serving as a catalyst for the continued evolution of the LLP@LHC physics program.

As machine learning agents interact more frequently with humans, it becomes increasingly evident that an agent trained solely for optimal task performance using performance-based feedback may violate societal norms or cause harm. Value alignment addresses this by ensuring intelligent agents exclusively pursue non-harmful, human-beneficial goals. We present a method for value-aligned reinforcement learning that trains an agent with a dual reward structure: a standard reward for task performance and an additional reward for normative behavior. This latter reward is derived from a pre-trained, value-aligned prior model capable of classifying text as either normative or non-normative. We demonstrate how adapting policy shaping techniques can effectively balance these two reward sources, resulting in policies that are both highly effective and perceived as more socially normative. Our evaluation tests this value-alignment approach across three interactive text-based environments, each designed to challenge agents with a primary task while simultaneously offering opportunities to engage in normative or altruistic behaviors outside that task.

Using approximately 37 $pb^{-1}$ of LHCb data from 2010, an effective $B^0_s\rightarrow K^+K^-$ lifetime measurement is reported. This value aids in constraining potential beyond the Standard Model contributions within the $B^0_s$ meson system and is derived through two complementary methods, yielding $\tau_{B^0_s\to K^+K^-} = 1.440 \pm 0.096 (stat) \pm 0.008 (syst) \pm 0.003 (model)$ ps.

This work investigates a variation of the target defense problem in which one defender must intercept a stream of arriving intruders. The intruders aim to breach the target's boundary while avoiding capture. Immediately after the current intruder is either captured or breaches the target, a new intruder emerges at a random position on a fixed circle enclosing the target. Consequently, the defender's position at the conclusion of one encounter serves as the starting position for the next, prompting both players to adopt strategies beneficial for the current and future rounds. Based on the information available to each player, the game is categorized into partial and full information phases. Assuming specific conditions regarding sensing and speed, we analyze strategies for both phases and derive equilibrium approaches for the defender and intruder to maximize the capture rate using concepts of the engagement surface and capture circle. Finally, we calculate the capture percentage for both finite and infinite sequences of intruders.

This study proposes a framework for the remote preparation of a two-particle state using either two Einstein-Podolsky-Rosen pairs or two partial entangled two-particle states as the quantum channel. We also determine the probability of successful remote state preparation.

The exact solution for the collision dynamics between hard spheres and cylindrical pores represents the simplest model of a regularly structured porous membrane. Nonequilibrium event-driven molecular dynamics simulations demonstrate that the permeability $P$ of hard spheres with diameter $\sigma$ passing through cylindrical pores of diameter $d$ adheres to a hindered diffusion mechanism driven by size exclusion, scaling as $P \propto (1-\sigma/d)^2$. Consequently, when separating binary mixtures of large and small particles, a linear correlation exists between $\alpha^{-1/2}$ and $P^{-1/2}$, where $\alpha$ denotes selectivity and $P$ denotes permeability for the smaller species. Furthermore, the mean permeability through polydisperse pore distributions is calculated by summing the individual pore permeabilities, weighted by each pore's area fraction relative to the total pore area.

This study introduces MagOD, a custom-built spectrophotometer integrating electromagnets specifically designed for analyzing suspensions of magnetotactic bacteria, though it remains applicable to other magnetic particles and cells. To facilitate replication, we provide open access to all 3D printing files for the enclosure, electronic schematics, PCB layouts, and the associated microcontroller software. Our performance benchmarks compare this new system against adapted commercial spectrophotometers. We demonstrate its utility by measuring bacterial absorbance based on orientation relative to the light path and by tracking reorientation speeds following a 90-degree magnetic field rotation. Additionally, we monitored magnetotactic bacterial culture growth for five days and assessed velocity distribution dynamics over a one-hour window. Despite its relatively simple construction and cost-effectiveness, MagOD extracts a diverse range of magnetic field-dependent parameters from magnetotactic suspensions, offering valuable tools for the research community to better understand and apply this fascinating microorganism.

The Extreme-ultraviolet Stellar Characterization for Atmospheric Physics and Evolution (ESCAPE) mission serves as an astrophysics Small Explorer designed to investigate the high-energy radiation surrounding the habitable zones of nearby stars. By utilizing ultraviolet spectroscopy—specifically in the EUV range of 80–825 \AA and the FUV range of 1280–1650 \AA—ESCAPE will conduct the first comprehensive analysis of stellar EUV conditions and coronal mass ejections, factors that are critical for rocky exoplanet habitability. During its 20-month operational phase, the mission aims to characterize stellar environments to pinpoint systems best suited for life, thereby creating a strategic roadmap for NASA's future life-detection endeavors. Achieving approximately two orders of magnitude higher efficiency in EUV performance than prior missions, ESCAPE utilizes a grazing incidence telescope connected to a combined EUV and FUV spectrograph. Its science instrument integrates advanced grazing incidence optical systems with photon-counting UV detectors, building upon legacy hardware from NASA's astrophysics, heliophysics, and planetary science programs. The mission operates on a versatile, high-heritage spacecraft bus provided by Ball Aerospace's BCP Small platform, with data archives managed by the Mikulski Archive for Space Telescopes (MAST).

Deep learning-based segmentation methods for computer vision often face limitations due to massive input sizes or constrained computational resources, typically leading to a common approach of uniformly downsampling images under the assumption that all pixels hold equal importance. This study reveals that such an assumption can degrade segmentation quality, as spatial regions vary in difficulty. To address this, we propose a learnable downsampling module optimized alongside the segmentation model in an end-to-end framework. We define the training objective as optimizing sampling density distributions based on low-resolution previews. To prevent degenerate outcomes—such as oversampling trivial areas like backgrounds—we introduce a regularization term that drives sampling locations to cluster around object boundaries. Our findings show that the module effectively learns to concentrate sampling on challenging regions, significantly enhancing performance. Experiments across high-resolution benchmarks for street views, aerial imagery, and medical data demonstrate substantial gains in the efficiency-accuracy trade-off compared to both uniform downsampling and two state-of-the-art alternative techniques.

Sketch-based image manipulation is an interactive editing process that alters images based on user-provided sketches. Current approaches typically frame this task as conditional inpainting, necessitating an additional mask from users to specify the area of change. In this setup, masked areas are treated as holes to be filled by an inpainting model guided by the sketch. While this formulation simplifies paired data generation via random masking and contour extraction, it complicates user interaction and ignores valuable information contained within the masked regions. Consequently, we propose a new paradigm called "mask-free local image manipulation," which relies solely on sketch inputs and utilizes the complete original image. Given an image and a sketch, our model autonomously identifies the target modification area and encodes it into a structure-agnostic style vector. A generator then synthesizes new image content using this style vector and the sketch. The final manipulated image is generated by blending the synthetic output into the identified modification region of the original image. The model supports self-supervised training by learning to reconstruct an image region from the style vector and sketch. This method delivers more intuitive and streamlined workflows compared to prior techniques, achieving superior results. Additional results, code, and an interactive demonstration can be found at \url{https://zengxianyu.github.io/sketchedit}.

This paper investigates information extraction techniques, specifically entity recognition and relation classification, within scientific literature on information technology. While publications offer critical insights into emerging scientific advancements, the efficient processing of the growing volume of data remains a time-intensive challenge. Consequently, the study proposes several modifications of existing methods tailored for the Russian language. The authors also report on experiments comparing a keyword extraction approach, a vocabulary-based method, and neural network-based models. Although annotated datasets for these tasks are readily available and widely used for English, comparable Russian resources have historically been absent from public domains. To address this gap, the paper introduces RuSERRC, a corpus of Russian scientific texts comprising 1600 documents, including 800 labeled for entities and six types of semantic relations. The dataset and associated models are accessible via https://github.com/iis-research-team, with the intention of supporting further research and the development of information extraction systems.

Transverse spherocity is an event structure observable that effectively separates processes into hard and soft components, corresponding to collisions with low and high numbers of multi-parton interactions (MPI), respectively. Recent LHC findings in small systems highlight the critical role of this variable for event classification. This contribution investigates identified particle production dynamics in Xe-Xe collisions at $\sqrt{s_{NN}}$ = 5.44 TeV using both the A Multi-Phase Transport (AMPT) model and the Angantyr model integrated into PYTHIA8. We present transverse momentum spectra for identified particles within soft (isotropic) and hard (jetty-like) event categories across various centrality bins.

For a quaternionic slice regular function $f$, we provide a straightforward and practical method to determine the coefficients of its spherical expansion at any point, expressing them via spherical and slice derivatives of the function itself. We subsequently compare these coefficients with those of the slice derivative $\partial_{c}f$, thereby deriving a countable family of differential equations that any slice regular function must satisfy. Each result is rigorously proven with full detail and supported by numerous examples; for certain findings, alternative proofs are also presented.

Symbolic regression encompasses a suite of methods designed to extract analytical expressions from data. By providing closed-form formulas, these approaches offer significant benefits, including the potential for scientific discovery of new laws, explainability, feature engineering, and rapid inference. In parallel, deep learning-based methods have demonstrated an exceptional capacity to model intricate patterns. This paper investigates the application of a recent end-to-end symbolic regression technique, known as the equation learner (EQL), to formulate an analytical equation for wind speed forecasting. The results demonstrate that a reasonable level of accuracy can be achieved for short-term forecasts using a limited set of features.

In the context of projective hyperplane arrangements, we examine sufficient conditions, based on combinatorial data, for determining the computability of monodromy eigenspaces within the first Milnor fiber cohomology for eigenvalues with an order $m>1$ (specifically ESV-calculability). Following Artin's theorem, this problem can be simplified to the scenario of line arrangements. However, these sufficient conditions frequently fail when the combinatorial structure exhibits high complexity or efficiency. To address this, we introduce the concepts of $m$-efficiency and $m$-complexity for $m\ge 3$. $m$-efficiency is defined as the average number of collinear points on a single line that have a multiplicity divisible by $m$. In numerous instances, if a sufficient condition holds and the $m$-efficiency is 2 or less, the condition is satisfied, though exceptions do occur, particularly when $m=3$. Furthermore, $m$-complexity is defined as the maximum number of edges connected to any single vertex in the corresponding $m$-graph. We demonstrate that a sufficient condition is satisfied whenever the $m$-complexity does not exceed $(m+1)/2$.

Program synthesis has emerged as a significant area of inquiry across academia, national laboratories, and industry. Although some promising advancements have been achieved, efforts directly targeted at scientific computing remain relatively constrained. This report surveys key developments in program synthesis within scientific computing, evaluates existing achievements, and proposes avenues for future research. These findings stem from the virtual Workshop on Program Synthesis for Scientific Computing, which took place on August 4–5, 2020 (https://prog-synth-science.github.io/2020/).

This work introduces Mitiq, a Python package designed to mitigate errors in noisy quantum computing. These techniques significantly reduce noise impacts on near-term devices by utilizing a combination of quantum sampling and classical post-processing, all with minimal overhead in quantum resources. Mitiq offers an extensible suite of mitigation strategies, featuring methods such as zero-noise extrapolation, probabilistic error cancellation, and Clifford data regression. The library supports compatibility with generic backends and integrates seamlessly with various quantum software frameworks. We outline Mitiq through code examples, highlighting its features and contribution protocols, and present multiple case studies demonstrating its application on IBM and Rigetti superconducting processors as well as noisy simulators.

Evaluating the expectation value of a generic observable $A\in{\mathbb{C}}^{2^n\times 2^n}$ using naive Pauli measurements necessitates calculating a substantial number of terms. To address this, we propose an "extended Bell measurement method" grounded in Bell measurements. This analytical approach efficiently partitions the $4^n$ matrix elements into no more than $2^{n+1}$ groups for simultaneous execution in $O(nd)$ time, where $d$ represents the count of $A$'s non-zero entries. The group count is notably reduced for band matrices; specifically, if the bandwidth $k$ scales as $O(n^c)$, the number of required groups drops to $O(n^{c+1})$. Furthermore, when non-zero entries densely populate the band, the variance becomes $O((n^{c+1}/2^n)\,{\rm tr}(A^2))$, a figure that is significantly lower than the variances associated with current methods. The protocol introduces only minimal additional circuit overhead per measurement: one Hadamard gate, one phase gate, and up to $n-1$ CNOT gates. Experimental validation on an IBM-Q platform demonstrates the scheme's computational efficiency and scalability relative to existing state-of-the-art techniques. Source code is accessible at https://github.com/ToyotaCRDL/extended-bell-measurements.

Retinal degenerative conditions lead to severe vision loss in over 10 million individuals globally, prompting the development of retinal prostheses designed to restore sight. Similar to cochlear implants, these devices electrically stimulate surviving retinal neurons to trigger visual percepts known as phosphenes. Although current prosthetic vision remains primitive, there is significant potential to enhance its utility by integrating advanced computer vision algorithms into image processing. Instead of striving for a complete restoration of "natural" vision, we propose leveraging state-of-the-art computational methods to improve visual performance. In this study, we synthesize deep learning-based scene simplification with a biologically validated computational model of the retina to realistically predict simulated prosthetic vision. We then assess how well these predictions support scene understanding among sighted subjects acting as virtual patients across diverse outdoor settings. Our findings indicate that object segmentation facilitates scene comprehension more effectively than models relying solely on visual saliency or monocular depth estimation. Furthermore, we emphasize the necessity of grounding theoretical predictions in biologically realistic models of phosphene morphology. Ultimately, this research could substantially advance the practical application of prosthetic vision for those blinded by retinal degeneration.

Quantum computing is transitioning from theory to practice, yet the implementation of physical qubits faces significant hurdles due to environmental noise. These pervasive quantum noises often degrade performance, driving extensive research into correction and mitigation strategies. However, is the impact of quantum noise always detrimental? We address this by introducing a framework known as quantum noise-induced reservoir computing, which demonstrates that certain abstract noise models can actually enhance information processing for temporal data. Through evaluation on various standard benchmarks, we analyzed the framework's information processing capacity and memory characteristics to elucidate its operational mechanism. Experimental validation on multiple IBM quantum processors yielded memory profiles consistent with theoretical models, confirming our findings. Notably, we discovered that the information processing capacity improves as quantum device noise levels and error rates increase. This research paves a new path for leveraging quantum computer noise, converting it into a powerful resource for sophisticated information processing.

This study examines two recent approaches designed to derive a priori lower bounds for the minima of general integral variational problems. Both techniques, which utilize either 'occupation measures' (Korda et al., Numerical Control: Part A) or a 'pointwise dual relaxation' procedure (Chernyavsky et al., arXiv:2110.03079), are demonstrated to yield identical lower bounds when a coercivity condition ensures strong duality. Through a minimax argument, we prove that these methods effectively compute the exact minimum for classes of problems involving one dimension, scalar values, or convex multidimensional spaces. Conversely, for generic problems, we conjecture that these methods fail to identify the true minimum, resulting in non-sharp bounds. This limitation is illustrated through two specific examples: the first is a one-dimensional, scalar problem with a non-convex constraint, while the second involves a multidimensional, non-convex formulation. The latter highlights the presence of nonlinear gradient field constraints in multiple dimensions that are overlooked by occupation measures but accounted for in the more rigorous theory of gradient Young measures, which is reviewed herein.

We introduce a direct metric for tripartite quantum correlations within arbitrary symmetric pure states comprising N correlated two-level atoms (qubits). By calculating the third-order moments of collective pseudo-spin operators using individual atomic operators, we demonstrate that all bipartite correlation terms among the atoms vanish, isolating exclusively the tripartite correlation terms. Our analysis reveals that these third-order moments consist solely of tripartite quantum correlations, facilitating the extraction and quantification of such correlations among the N atoms. Furthermore, we establish necessary and sufficient conditions for the existence of tripartite quantum correlations in these multi-atomic systems and propose an experimental method for determining the third-order moments of the pseudo-spin operators in these assemblies.

Much prior research has centered on narrowing the performance disparity between high- and low-resource languages, with typological features from databases like the World Atlas of Language Structures (WALS) being a primary candidate due to their availability even for languages with scarce data. Nevertheless, previous studies have only identified marginal gains from incorporating such typological information. Our hypothesis posits that a model operating in a cross-lingual setting automatically extracts these typological cues from the data, thereby rendering explicit feature usage redundant. To test this, we "blind" a model to typological information to examine the effects on cross-lingual sharing and overall performance. Our approach utilizes a cross-lingual architecture where the parameters controlling inter-language sharing are learned during training. Our findings demonstrate that (i) blocking the model from leveraging typology drastically lowers performance, and (ii) a control experiment confirms that guiding sharing based on typology yields modest performance improvements.

This paper investigates two graphically distinct structures—the zero divisor graph $\Gamma(C_c(X))$ and the comaximal graph $\Gamma_2^{'}(C_c(X))$—associated with the ring $C_c(X)$ of real-valued continuous functions with countable ranges defined on a Hausdorff zero-dimensional space $X$. Although these graphs appear different, they share several topological properties, including diameter, girth, connectedness, and triangulation or hypertriangulation characteristics. However, the analysis demonstrates that the zero divisor graph of an intermediate ring $A_c(X)$ within $C_c(X)$ is complemented precisely when the space of its minimal prime ideals is compact. Furthermore, $\Gamma(C_c(X))$ itself is complemented if and only if its subgraph $\Gamma(A_c(X))$ is. Conversely, the comaximal graph of $C_c(X)$ is complemented exactly when the comaximal graph of its over-ring $C(X)$ is; this condition for $C(X)$ holds if and only if $X$ is a $P$-space. Notably, for a broad category of spaces (specifically, perfectly normal, strongly zero-dimensional spaces that are not $P$-spaces), the graphs $\Gamma(C_c(X))$ and $\Gamma_2^{'}(C_c(X))$ are proven to be non-isomorphic. By appropriately defining the quotient of a graph, the study establishes that for a discrete space $X$, these two graphs are isomorphic (and equivalent to those of $C(X)$) whenever $X$ is at most countable. Additionally, assuming the continuum hypothesis, the converse of this isomorphism result is also valid.

This study investigates neutrino signals generated by proton decays induced by Grand Unified Theory (GUT) monopoles within the Sun. The Super-Kamiokande experiment has been evaluated using three standard proton decay channels: $p ightarrow e^+ + (ho^0, \eta, \omega...) ightarrow \pi^+$, $p ightarrow \mu^+ K^0$, and $p ightarrow  ar{
u}_e \pi^+$. Monopole-induced neutrinos originate from the interactions and subsequent decays of these proton breakdown products. To derive neutrino energy spectra, Geant4 software was employed to simulate the propagation of daughter particles through the dense solar core. Our findings indicate that the charge exchange reaction $K^0 + p ightarrow K^+ + n$, followed by the decay of a stopped $K^+$ into $\mu^+ 
u_\mu$, can generate a significant flux of monoenergetic 236 MeV $
u_\mu$ neutrinos. Given this distinctive capability, the decay mode $p ightarrow \mu^+ K^0$ offers the highest discovery potential for most parameter spaces compared to the other modes. Furthermore, we outline the sensitivity limits of Super-Kamiokande regarding monopole flux for each of the three analyzed proton decay pathways.

The rapid ionization of a sizable molecule can trigger a correlation-driven phenomenon known as charge migration, characterized by swift alterations in electron density. Directly capturing this redistribution within the few-femtosecond to attosecond timeframe constitutes real-time observation of molecular electron correlation. Although such a process lacks experimental confirmation to date, we present a time-resolved investigation into charge migration in the bio-molecule adenine following ionization by an attosecond pulse spanning 15–35 eV. We demonstrate that the formation of intact doubly charged adenine through a delayed, laser-induced second ionization event serves as the hallmark of a charge localization mechanism driven by many-body excitations, a conclusion validated by first-principles time-dependent simulations. These results establish novel avenues for controlling molecular reactivity on electronic timescales.

The study applies the coupling-constant metamorphosis to modified extended Hamiltonians and establishes sufficient conditions under which the transformed high-degree first integral of the resulting Hamiltonian is computed via the same algorithm used for the original extended Hamiltonian. As case studies, the Post-Winternitz system and the two-dimensional caged anisotropic oscillator are examined.

The simplicity of inflationary supergravity alpha-attractor models hinges on Volkov-Akulov fermions, typically represented as nilpotent superfields. This work investigates employing the double-copy method to formulate Dirac-Born-Infeld-Volkov-Akulov (DBIVA) theories within supergravity. While a color-dual bootstrap successfully derives scattering amplitudes involving pions and vectors up to five-point tree-level order across all mass-dimension levels, it necessitates the inclusion of a $Tr(F^3)$ operator. Recent findings indicate that gauge theories containing this operator demand an infinite series of higher-derivative operators to satisfy color-kinematics duality. Consequently, the most conservative approach to constructing the DBVIA + pure Poincare supergravity double-copy via the adjoint formalism suggests a need for UV completion into a family of theories coupling DBVIA-like particles to Weyl-Einstein supergravity. Additionally, we identify an alternative route to achieve adjoint double-copy for color-dual gauged pions; while this avoids the need for a tower of higher-derivative corrections, it necessitates the sacrifice of exchange symmetry among scalars.

Building upon the separate BI-RME and ECLOUD (PyECLOUD) codes, we are creating a new integrated simulation framework designed to model the combined influence of charged particle beams and microwaves on an electron cloud. Potential applications for this tool include investigating microwave signal degradation in telecommunication satellites caused by electron clouds; analyzing microwave transmission methods utilized in particle accelerators for electron cloud diagnostics; examining microwave emissions generated by electron clouds within magnetic fields; and exploring strategies to suppress electron cloud formation in accelerators through the injection of microwaves with specific frequencies and amplitudes. Several preliminary simulation outcomes are presented.

Our team intends to conduct a comprehensive energy demand response experiment within an office building. While this project is promising and beneficial to the community, acquiring training data for the reinforcement learning agent involves high costs and is resource-limited. This study investigates how offline training can reduce both data expenses and accelerate convergence while lowering implementation overhead. We propose two methods: using pretraining with simulated tasks to provide a warm start for the model, and employing a planning model designed to simulate real-world rewards. The results illustrate the effectiveness of offline reinforcement learning for achieving efficient price-setting in energy demand response scenarios.

This article outlines the technical specifications and features of the magnetic shield engineered for 20-inch PMTs within the low-background OSIRIS facility. Its design incorporates a ribbon of amorphous alloy possessing exceptional magnetic permeability, enabling highly effective screening of the Earth's magnetic field using a relatively small quantity of material. In low-background facility construction, minimizing material mass is critical for controlling radioactive backgrounds, and the use of amorphous materials offers a cost-effective alternative to other screening techniques.

Prostate cancer (PCa) ranks among the most prevalent and aggressive malignancies globally. The Gleason score (GS) serves as the conventional standard for categorizing prostate cancer and is the most dependable approach for assessing disease severity and guiding treatment plans. Pathologists evaluate the structural arrangement of cancer cells within the prostate, assigning a value on a scale from 6 to 10. However, automatic analysis of prostate whole-slide images (WSIs) is typically framed as a binary classification task, thereby overlooking the nuanced distinctions provided by the Gleason grading system. This paper introduces a probabilistic deep learning framework for ordinal classification capable of estimating the Gleason score directly from prostate WSIs. By treating this challenge as an ordinal regression problem via a differentiable probabilistic model, the study achieves both enhanced result interpretability and superior accuracy compared to traditional deep classification and regression architectures.

This research examines phase equilibria in a fluid confined within an open capillary slit, created by positioning a finite-length wall (height $H$) a distance $L$ from a macroscopic surface. The system exhibits complex phase behaviors resulting from the interplay between two distinct capillary condensation mechanisms: corner filling and meniscus depinning transitions, the dominance of which varies with the aspect ratio $a=L/H$. In long capillaries where $a<2/\pi$, condensation follows type I behavior, featuring menisci pinned at the upper edges by an edge contact angle. For intermediate capillaries ($2/\pi<a<1$), the condensation type depends on the contact angle; it can be type I or type II, the latter characterized by menisci overflowing into the reservoir without pinning. In short capillaries where $a>1$, condensation is consistently type II. Across all regimes, capillary condensation is entirely inhibited when contact angles are sufficiently large. We identify an additional continuous phase transition within the condensed liquid-like state, linked to the depinning of menisci as they curve over the slit's open upper edges. We derive finite-size scaling predictions for these transitions and the connecting phase boundaries, relating them to fluctuation theories of wetting and filling. Finally, we validate multiple predictions using a fully microscopic Density Functional Theory capable of resolving the molecular details of both condensation types and their suppression.

While large pre-trained code models have achieved remarkable progress across numerous coding tasks, their broad integration into developers' daily workflows is hindered by high memory consumption and slow execution on personal devices, complicating deployment and diminishing user experience. To address this, we introduce Compressor, a novel technique capable of compressing large pre-trained code models into extremely compact versions with negligible performance loss. Compressor approaches the creation of tiny models by simplifying the original architecture through a search for a significantly smaller structure that maintains architectural similarity to the pre-trained model. Guided by a genetic algorithm (GA) strategy, the simplification process optimizes for higher Giga floating-point operations (GFLOPs)—an indicator of computational cost—subject to a strict target size constraint, leveraging the insight that greater computational cost generally correlates with enhanced power. Following this, knowledge distillation is employed to train the reduced model by using unlabeled data to generate teacher labels from the large model for the small model.
