Evaluated on CodeBERT and GraphCodeBERT across vulnerability prediction and clone detection tasks, Compressor successfully compresses these models to approximately 3 MB, a reduction of 160 times their original size. The results demonstrate that the compressed models achieve inference speeds 4.31 times and 4.15 times faster than their original counterparts, respectively, without sacrificing performance.

The study introduces a rare dual-ray phenomenon of resonant light scattering in periodic metasurfaces designed to generate robust non-specular reflection. This metasurface consists of silicon nanodisk arrays positioned on a thin silica-on-metal substrate. Numerical simulations demonstrate low-loss, non-specular resonant reflection capable of functioning across various incident directions and polarizations. The research derives the requirements for an autocollimation scattering scheme and highlights the observation of non-specular reflected rays that exist outside the plane of incidence. Furthermore, adjusting the dielectric substrate's thickness is identified as a method to regulate the frequency bandwidth of non-specular reflection. Additionally, the intensity ratio between specular and non-specular reflected rays can be manipulated by altering the angle of incidence or the incident wave's polarization.

This work introduces novel differential privacy frameworks for data products subject to simultaneous enforcement of external invariants and integer constraints. Such requirements are critical in real-world private data curation tasks, exemplified by the public release of the 2020 U.S. Decennial Census, presenting significant challenges to generating statistically useful, provably private outputs. We formalize the privacy guarantees under these conditions with \emph{integer subspace differential privacy} and establish its composition and post-processing properties. To overcome the difficulty of sampling from highly restricted discrete spaces, we develop two unbiased additive mechanisms—generalized Laplace and generalized Gaussian mechanisms—derived by solving the associated Diophantine equations. These mechanisms offer superior accuracy, characterized by error distributions with sub-exponential and sub-Gaussian tail probabilities, respectively. For practical implementation, we design an MCMC algorithm and validate its empirical convergence by estimating upper bounds on total variation distance through $L$-lag coupling. The efficacy of our approach is demonstrated through a synthetic problem involving intersecting invariants, the release of a sensitive contingency table with fixed margins, and the 2010 Census county-level data with mandated state population totals.

Categories such as animal or furniture are acquired early in life and serve a crucial role in how individuals process, organize, and communicate their understanding of the world. While such categories exist universally across cultures, enabling the efficient representation of worldly complexity with strong community agreement on their nature, current models of category learning and representation often rely on limited data from small-scale experiments involving artificially constrained features and specific demographic groups—typically Western, educated, native English speakers like U.S. college students. This research investigates whether categorization models generalize when applied to (a) rich, noisy data reflecting the environments humans actually inhabit, and (b) across different languages and cultures. We introduce a Bayesian cognitive model capable of jointly learning categories and their structured representations from natural language text, which facilitates (a) large-scale performance evaluation and (b) application across a diverse linguistic landscape. Our findings demonstrate that meaningful categories encompassing hundreds of concepts, along with richly structured featural representations, emerge consistently across languages. This work highlights the potential of combining recent advances in computational modeling with large-scale naturalistic datasets for cognitive science.

In condensed-matter physics, electronic Mott insulators have been a significant area of study because of their complex connection to high-temperature superconductivity. However, unlike atomic systems where Mott phases have been recently demonstrated for both fermions and bosons, a solid-state signature of a Mott insulator composed of bosons has yet to be discovered. In this study, we reveal such a signature by investigating the Bose-Hubbard Hamiltonian using semiconductor excitons trapped within two-dimensional lattices. We focus on the regime where on-site interactions are similar in magnitude to the energy gap between confined lattice states. Our observations indicate that Mott phases are reachable, specifically when lattice sites are uniformly filled with at most two excitons. Furthermore, our methodology enables the on-demand programming of the exciton confining lattice geometry. This adaptability, together with the long-range dipolar interactions between excitons, opens a new pathway to investigate many-body phases that spontaneously break lattice symmetry.

This study examines exclusive $\pi^-\Delta^{++}$ electroproduction using the handbag framework, where helicity amplitudes decompose into hard partonic interactions and generalized parton distributions (GPDs). We establish $p-\Delta$ transversity GPDs, adopting helicity non-flip GPDs from existing literature. For numerical predictions of observables, we apply large-$N_C$ constraints to link specific $p-\Delta$ GPDs to those of the proton, ignoring remaining GPDs. Additionally, we compute twist-2 and twist-3 subprocess amplitudes by incorporating quark transverse momenta alongside Sudakov suppressions. Finally, we forecast the partial cross sections for $\gamma^*p\to \pi^-\Delta^{++}$ within the large-$N_C$ limit.

Quantum walks serve as robust tools for developing quantum search and sampling algorithms, specifically for constructing stationary quantum states. However, the success rates of these algorithms are currently significantly distant from unity. While amplitude amplification is typically employed to boost these probabilities, it introduces the problem of "soufflé" dynamics, where success rates oscillate; stopping precisely at the optimal step is critical for maximizing success. If the algorithm runs too long, success probabilities can decline, creating practical challenges when the ideal step count is unknown. This work introduces generalized interpolated quantum walks, capable of both enhancing the success probability of search algorithms and mitigating the souffle issue. By integrating generalized interpolated quantum walks with quantum fast-forwarding, we reduce the number of walk operator calls from $\Theta((\varepsilon^{-1})\sqrt{\Heg})$ to $\Theta(\log(\varepsilon^{-1})\sqrt{\Heg})$ and decrease the required ancilla qubits from $\Theta(\log(\varepsilon^{-1})+\log\sqrt{\Heg})$ to $\Theta(\log\log(\varepsilon^{-1})+\log\sqrt{\Heg})$. This combination improves success probability while entirely avoiding the souffle problem, where $\varepsilon$ represents precision and $\Heg$ denotes the classical hitting time. Furthermore, we demonstrate that generalized interpolated quantum walks can also refine the construction of quantum states representing stationary distributions. Finally, we present an application utilizing generalized interpolated quantum walks to generate a slowly evolving Markov chain sequence, a requisite step for adiabatic stationary state preparation.

This work employs the functional renormalization group method to analyze a $\mathcal{N}=1$ supersymmetric gauge theory comprising a vector $U(1)$ superfield coupled to a single chiral superfield. We demonstrate that the nonrenormalization theorem remains valid at the leading order of the supercovariant derivative expansion for the fields. Furthermore, we calculate the beta functions and examine the fixed point behavior under a local potential approximation, with additional discussion regarding the regulators used.

The lattice size $\operatorname{ls_\Delta}(P)$ of a lattice polytope $P$ serves as a crucial invariant; originally defined in the context of bounding the total and bi-degrees of algebraic curves, it was used more implicitly within geometric combinatorics prior to that. This paper demonstrates that for any empty lattice polytope $P\subset\mathbb{R}^3$, a specific reduced basis of $\mathbb{Z}^3$ exists to compute its lattice size. This finding enables a rapid algorithm for calculating $\operatorname{ls_\Delta}(P)$ in such cases. Furthermore, the study extends these results to another category of lattice polytopes $P\subset\mathbb{R}^3$ with lattice width one. Finally, the authors present a counterexample proving that the stated result fails for general lattice polytopes $P\subset\mathbb{R}^3$ possessing a lattice width of one.

In 2017, Colorado implemented Risk-Limiting Audits (RLAs) throughout the state, utilizing both ballot-level comparison and ballot-polling techniques. However, these audits were limited to races contained within a single county, as methods to efficiently audit cross-county contests or combine polling with level-by-level comparisons were unavailable at the time. The existing audit software (RLATool) required upgrades to handle races spanning county boundaries and to process small contests more effectively. This paper addresses those specific needs by outlining highly simple yet inefficient approaches, more efficient strategies that integrate ballot polling and comparisons via stratified sampling, and alternative methods that merge these audit types without requiring stratified sampling. The conclusion offers recommendations and demonstrates the proposed method using comparative examples against current practices. Additionally, open-source code and interactive Jupyter notebooks are provided to implement these methods and facilitate further analysis.

Recent advancements in self-supervision have successfully produced feature representations comparable to those achieved through full supervision, offering benefits such as enhanced robustness and improved out-of-distribution detection. This paper presents an empirical analysis of how self-supervised learning—whether employed as a pre-training strategy or integrated into adversarial training—influences a model's resilience against $l_2$ and $l_{\infty}$ adversarial attacks as well as natural image corruptions. While self-supervision does boost robustness, the specifics matter greatly. Merely adding self-supervision loss alongside adversarial training improves accuracy only for perturbations with magnitudes similar to or smaller than the training budget ($\epsilon_{train}$). Conversely, when evaluated against stronger attacks where $\epsilon_{test} \ge \epsilon_{train}$, model accuracy declines; notably, increasing the weight of the supervision loss exacerbates this performance drop, ultimately harming robustness. We examine different approaches to integrating self-supervision into adversarial training and find that using self-supervised loss to jointly optimize network parameters and generate adversarial examples yields the most significant robustness gains, effectively functioning as a form of ensemble adversarial training. Although pre-training with self-supervision outperforms random weight initialization during adversarial training, incorporating self-supervision directly into the adversarial training process itself provides no advantage in terms of either model accuracy or robustness.

This article serves as a follow-up to Shu-Xue-Yao's study in \cite{BYY} on enhanced groups and associated dualities within type $A$. We extend this inquiry to examine enhanced dualities for classical groups of type $B$, $C$, and $D$. To establish these results, we first define an enhanced Brauer algebra. Relying on Proposition \ref{B dual}, we readily derive restricted and Levi dualities, which in turn provide a natural framework for parabolic duality. Furthermore, we present a specific instance in Section \ref{3} supported by detailed explicit computations.

Bayesian optimization typically requires "inner optimization" over a non-convex, highly multi-modal acquisition function that can be non-differentiable and resistant to local numerical optimizers; consequently, discrete searches over random candidates are often employed. We introduce the use of Delaunay triangulation-based candidates derived from the current input design, referred to as "tricands." We outline their construction and empirically demonstrate that, on both synthetic and real simulation benchmarks, tricands outperform both numerically optimized acquisitions and random candidate methods while also integrating well into hybrid schemes.

Recent years have seen quantum control techniques for three-level systems emerge as a vital area of inquiry within quantum information science and technology. This work provides numerical simulations of quantum process tomography using realistic experimental parameters for both STIRAP (stimulated Raman adiabatic passage) and saSTIRAP (superadiabatic STIRAP). To achieve this, we identify an appropriate operator space basis composed of the identity operator and the eight Gell-Mann operators, allowing for the calculation of process matrices consisting of 81 elements ($9 \times 9$). Our analysis covers these findings under both ideal, decoherence-free conditions and scenarios relevant to actual experiments that include decoherence.

This document summarizes the most recent ATLAS experiment findings concerning top-quark pair production accompanied by a photon, based on proton-proton collision data collected at the LHC with a centre-of-mass energy of 13 TeV. The report covers both inclusive and differential cross-section measurements across single-lepton and dilepton final states, defined within a fiducial volume that matches the detector's acceptance.

We have identified a novel cosmological signal known as the Doppler-boosted Cosmic Infrared Background (DB-CIB). This phenomenon results from the peculiar motions of galaxies, which emit thermal dust contributing to the cosmic infrared background (CIB). As an independent probe of the cosmic velocity field, DB-CIB is closely analogous to the kinematic Sunyaev-Zel'dovich (kSZ) effect. Unlike the kSZ effect, DB-CIB is not subject to the 'kSZ optical depth degeneracy,' rendering it immune to the complex astrophysics of galaxy formation. We predict that DB-CIB will be detectable through cross-correlations between CCAT-Prime and DESI-like experiments. Furthermore, we demonstrate that DB-CIB functions as a new CMB foreground that could introduce bias into future kSZ cross-correlations unless properly accounted for.

Multi-agent Markov Decision Processes (MMDPs) have proven effective for modeling sequential decision-making in cooperative multi-agent environments. While various algorithms based on centralized and decentralized planning have emerged, the dynamic nature of the environment, combined with the exponential expansion of joint action and state spaces, hinders their ability to ensure both efficiency and scalability. Recently, the centralized FV-MCTS-MP and the decentralized *Alternate maximization with Behavioural Cloning* (ABC) algorithms demonstrated strong performance in solving MMDPs; however, the former fails to adapt to dynamic environments, and the latter cannot handle a lack of inter-agent communication. In response, we present SiCLOP, a simulation-based online planning algorithm designed for cooperative multi-agent scenarios. SiCLOP integrates Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) with Coordination Graphs (CG) and Graph Neural Networks (GCN) to learn cooperative strategies, delivering real-time solutions to MMDP problems. Furthermore, it enhances scalability by effectively pruning the action space. Unlike its predecessors, SiCLOP incorporates transfer learning, allowing agents trained in one setting to operate in others. We also provide a theoretical analysis of the algorithm's convergence within multi-agent contexts. Our extensive empirical evaluations demonstrate that SiCLOP significantly surpasses existing state-of-the-art online planning methods.

We introduce the 1-100 GeV spectral energy distribution (SED) for 148 recently discovered high-synchrotron-peaked blazars (HSPs) from the First Brazil-ICRANet Gamma-ray Blazar catalogue (1BIGB) identified by Fermi-LAT. The majority of these 1BIGB sources are absent from prior Fermi-LAT catalogues, making this the initial presentation of their gamma-ray spectral characteristics and a substantial expansion of the known gamma-ray blazar population. Given that the sample was initially selected based on excess signals within the 0.3-500 GeV range, these objects are considered promising TeV blazar candidates potentially observable by the upcoming Very-High-Energy (VHE) gamma-ray facility, CTA. Our flux estimates utilize PASS8 data integrated across more than nine years of Fermi-LAT observations. Additionally, we revisit the broadband fit spanning 0.3-500 GeV originally detailed in the 1BIGB paper, updating the power-law parameters using the latest available Fermi-LAT dataset, and assess the significance of these sources for VHE population studies involving both current instruments and the future CTA. To evaluate CTA detectability, we extrapolate the gamma-ray SEDs of a selected subsample to higher energies, accounting for extragalactic background light absorption, and compare these extrapolations against published CTA sensitivity curves. We provide an in-depth discussion of two notable members of the sample, 1BIGB J224910.6-130002 and 1BIGB J194356.2+211821. Finally, all previously unpublished gamma-ray SEDs presented here are made accessible to the public through the Brazilian Science Data Center (BSDC) at CBPF in Rio de Janeiro.

This document summarizes the findings of the Computational Frontier topical group regarding end-user analysis for Snowmass 2021. In this context, end-user analysis involves extracting physics results from reconstructed and simulated experimental data. High-energy physics experiments generate systems that execute common calibration, simulation, and reconstruction tasks, yielding shared data samples. These comprehensive samples are subsequently refined into various analysis datasets, often tailored for specific physics topics through trigger mechanisms or data object selection. Analyzers (end-users) then process these datasets to derive physics results. Community consensus led to the classification of the end-user analysis ensemble into five categories: Analysis Ecosystems, Analysis Models, Dataset Bookkeeping and Formats, Collaborative Software, and Training. We outline the findings and recommendations associated with these critical areas influencing end-user analysis.

We establish that, for smooth projective families of varieties with a good minimal model where the base has dimension no greater than five and a non-negative Kodaira dimension, the variation constitutes a lower bound for the base's Kodaira dimension. This result confirms the Kebekus–Kovács conjecture in the case where the base space dimension is at most five.
